metaTitle: Does Lysol Kill Bed Bugs? What the Label Says
metaDescription: Lysol is a disinfectant, not a bed bug insecticide, and its label names no insects. See what a direct spray can do, what it misses and what to use.
h1: Does Lysol Kill Bed Bugs? What the Label, the Research and the EPA Say
dek: Lysol is a disinfectant, not an insecticide. Here is what its label claims, what a direct spray can and cannot do, and how to check whether any product is labeled for bed bugs.
excerpt: Lysol is a germ-killing disinfectant, and its label names no insects. What a direct spray may do, what it misses, and how to check a product's label for bed bugs.

quickAnswer.lead: **Lysol is a disinfectant, not a bed bug insecticide, and the label EPA accepted for it in January 2025 claims germs, mold and odors but names no insects.** A bug soaked directly may die, yet no source reviewed measured it, and a spray on exposed surfaces misses the bugs and eggs hidden in seams and cracks. [EPA's guidance](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/stay-legal-and-safe-treating-bed-bugs) is to use a registered product labeled for bed bugs.
bullets: The EPA-accepted label for Lysol Disinfectant Spray (Reg. No. 777-99, January 2025) lists ethanol at 58 percent and alkyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium saccharinate at 0.10 percent, and its performance claims concern microbes, mold and odor.
Its directions call for keeping a pre-cleaned hard surface wet for 3 or 10 minutes to disinfect, limit fabric use to a spot treatment that is not saturated, and carry a flammability warning.

In a Rutgers lab test, two detergent sprays sold for bed bugs were among the products that caused 0 to 30 percent mortality in directly sprayed nymphs over 10 days, while fewer than 10 percent of the water-sprayed control nymphs died.
EPA has registered more than 300 products for use against bed bugs, in seven chemical classes.
CDC counted 111 illnesses from bed bug insecticide use in seven states from 2003 to 2010, including one death.

body.text: Does Lysol kill bed bugs?

Not as a bed bug treatment. Lysol is a germ-killing disinfectant, the EPA-accepted label for it makes no claim about insects, and nothing reviewed for this page shows that it can clear an infestation. A bed bug that is soaked directly may die, but the bugs that decide whether an infestation ends are the ones hidden in seams, cracks and furniture, along with the eggs, and a spray on exposed surfaces does not reach them.

The rest of this guide covers what the label says, what the closest laboratory evidence shows, how to read any product label for a bed bug claim, and what to do in place of spraying. [The complete bed bug guide](/learn/bed-bugs) puts every treatment option in one place.
What does the Lysol label actually say?

The label claims germs, mold, mildew and odors, and it never mentions an insect. That is the finding from the master label EPA accepted on January 13, 2025 for [EPA Reg. No. 777-99](https://www3.epa.gov/pesticides/chem_search/ppls/000777-00099-20250113.pdf), a product registered under the name Brace whose approved claims call it Lysol Disinfectant Spray. Its active ingredients are ethanol at 58 percent and alkyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium saccharinate at 0.10 percent, and the organisms it names are bacteria, viruses and fungi.

Lysol is a brand name on many products, labels are amended over time, and a master label carries optional wording that a given can may not print. Treat this one as a worked example and read the label on your own can the same way.

head: On the label
What it means for bed bugs
rows: Claims: sanitizes against bacteria, disinfects against bacteria, viruses and fungi, controls mold and mildew, deodorizes
The performance claims are about microbes, mold or smell. No insect is named anywhere on the label.
Hard-surface directions: pre-clean the surface, hold the can 6 to 8 inches away, spray for 3 to 4 seconds until covered with mist, and keep the surface visibly wet for 3 or 10 minutes to disinfect
These steps support a germ-killing claim. None of them describes treating an insect, a seam or a crack.
Fabric directions: spot treatment only; spray until wet, do not saturate, leave for 30 seconds to sanitize or 10 minutes to disinfect, then air dry
A light spot spray against germs is the opposite of soaking a mattress seam to drown insects.

Surfaces: hard surfaces include bed frames, bed or box springs and plastic mattress covers; soft-surface sites include bedding, linen, cushions, upholstered couches and an entry written as Mattress (Cover). Not for polished wood, painted surfaces, leather, rayon fabrics, acrylic plastics, silk, rayon acetate or satin
Bedroom items appear as places to kill germs. The label attaches no pest claim to any of them.
Hazard: flammable, contents under pressure; keep away from heat, sparks and open flame; causes moderate eye irritation; do not spray in eyes or on skin
The label asks users to keep the product away from heat and off skin, which is hard to square with soaking a bed.
Legal line: using the product in a manner inconsistent with its labeling is a violation of federal law
Using it on insects is not a use the label describes.

body.text: The bed frame and box springs on that list are there as hard surfaces to disinfect, and the bedding and mattress entries are there as fabrics to spot-treat against germs. Those are germ claims, not bed bug claims.
Could soaking a bed bug in Lysol kill it?

Possibly some, but there is no measured kill rate for Lysol to quote. The label makes no claim about insects, and none of the government or university sources reviewed for this page tested Lysol on bed bugs. The label does list ethanol, an alcohol, at 58 percent as an active ingredient, and the university research on how alcohol performs is covered in [the guide to rubbing alcohol and bed bugs](/blog/does-alcohol-kill-bed-bugs).

The nearest controlled evidence comes from Rutgers University. In [a 2014 study in the Journal of Economic Entomology](https://archive.sebs.rutgers.edu/wp-content/uploads/Singh2014Essentialoilsbedbugcontrol.pdf), researchers used a laboratory spray tower to spray fourth- and fifth-stage bed bug nymphs at a rate the authors call a standard point of runoff, and then watched them for 10 days. Two detergent-based sprays sold for bed bugs, Bed Bug 911 and Eradicator, were among the products that caused 0 to 30 percent mortality, while fewer than 10 percent of the nymphs sprayed with water died. Of the 11 non-synthetic products tested, the study's abstract says only two, EcoRaider and Bed Bug Patrol, caused more than 90 percent mortality of nymphs in both the direct spray and the forced-exposure residue tests.

That study did not include Lysol, and those products contain different ingredients, so it cannot supply a number for Lysol. What it shows is narrower: a bug that has been thoroughly wetted is not necessarily a dead bug, even with sprays made and marketed for the job.
Why won't Lysol get rid of an infestation?
Much of the problem is out of a spray's reach, and nothing on the label suggests it leaves behind anything that works on insects. Three gaps stand out.
Hidden bugs are out of reach

The Rutgers authors note that their results came from ideal conditions in which every bug was sprayed directly or exposed to the treatment, while in real homes bed bugs hide in cracks, crevices, creases and many other places where a spray may not land on them. The guide to [where bed bugs hide](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide) walks through the usual hiding places, starting with the bed.
Eggs are a separate problem

Of the five essential oil products the Rutgers team tested on eggs, only EcoRaider caused high egg mortality, about 87 percent after 14 days, and the other four had little effect. The two conventional insecticides in the same test, Temprid SC and Demand CS, killed 58 and 67 percent of eggs. The Lysol label makes no egg claim, and no source reviewed shows that a disinfectant affects eggs. A separate guide explains [why heat succeeds where sprays miss eggs](/blog/how-to-kill-bed-bug-eggs-canada).
A disinfectant film is not a residual

The label's disinfecting claims depend on keeping a surface wet for a set number of minutes, and it says nothing about killing insects that cross the dried surface later. Even products made for bed bugs differ widely in what they leave behind. In the Rutgers choice test, where nymphs could walk onto or away from treated fabric that had dried overnight, residue from the conventional insecticide Temprid SC had killed 90 percent of them after 10 days, compared with 10 percent for Bed Bug Patrol and under 2 percent for EcoRaider.
Is it safe to spray Lysol on a mattress or bedding?

A light spot spray for germs is a use the current label describes, but soaking a mattress or bedding to kill bugs is not, and the label carries warnings that matter in a bedroom. Its fabric directions are for spot treatment only: spray until wet, do not saturate, leave the fabric for 30 seconds to sanitize or 10 minutes to disinfect, and let it air dry. The label also says not to use the spray on silk, rayon acetate or satin, and to test a hidden area of fabric first.

The warnings apply however the can is used. The label says the contents are flammable and under pressure, that the can should be kept away from heat, sparks and open flame, and that exposure to temperatures above 130°F may cause bursting. Its precautions say the spray causes moderate eye irritation and should not be sprayed in eyes or on skin.

body.title: Keep flammables away from heat
body.text: University of Florida Extension says not to attempt a home heat treatment, particularly in combination with flammable materials such as alcohol, and reports that combining heat with do-it-yourself products and home remedies has resulted in structurally destructive fires. EPA lists do-it-yourself heating among the practices that are legal but not safe. Do not pair a flammable spray with a heater, a hair dryer or an open flame.

If the product gets in the eyes, the label says to hold the eye open and rinse slowly and gently with water for 15 to 20 minutes, removing contact lenses after the first 5 minutes, and to call a poison control center or doctor for treatment advice.

Whether an insecticide may go on a mattress at all depends on its own label, which is a narrower question than what is sold for bed bugs. [The mattress guide](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress) covers which pesticides are and are not labeled for mattresses.
How can you tell whether a product is labeled for bed bugs?

Look for bed bugs named in the label's directions, because an EPA registration number alone does not mean a product is approved for them. The Lysol disinfectant carries the number 777-99 and still never mentions bed bugs. [EPA's guidance on staying legal and safe](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/stay-legal-and-safe-treating-bed-bugs) tells people to buy EPA-registered pesticides labeled for bed bug control and to look for the EPA registration number on the label, so a product needs both.

items: Find the EPA Reg. No. on the label. On the Lysol label it reads 777-99.
Read the pest list in the directions for use. Bed bugs have to be named. If they are not, the label gives no bed bug directions to follow.

Check where the label allows use. EPA lists using a pesticide labeled for outdoor use among the practices that are not legal, along with applying a pesticide to a bed, furniture or clothing when those surfaces are not on the label, so confirm indoor use and the specific places you plan to treat.

Follow the amount and the interval. EPA also lists using too much, or applying more often than the label allows, as not legal, and it puts repeated spraying whenever a bug turns up on its list of practices that are legal but not safe.
Use EPA's bed bug product search tool. [EPA's guide to bed bug pesticides](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/pesticides-control-bed-bugs) recommends it for finding a registered product.

Ask before you apply. The same EPA guide suggests consulting a pest management professional to inspect the home, and says the Cooperative Extension Service office in your area can help with choosing an appropriate pesticide.

body.text: What is actually labeled for bed bugs?

EPA says it has registered more than 300 products for use against bed bugs, in seven chemical classes: pyrethrins, pyrethroids, desiccants, biochemicals, pyrroles, neonicotinoids and insect growth regulators.

Desiccants deserve a closer look because the same substances are also sold for other uses. EPA says they work by destroying the waxy protective coating on a bed bug, that bed bugs cannot become resistant to them the way they can to pesticides with other modes of action, and that their use is limited to cracks and crevices to reduce the inhalation risk. Diatomaceous earth and boric acid are examples, but EPA says it is critical to use only desiccants that are registered by EPA and labeled for bed bug control, because versions intended for other uses, such as food-grade or swimming pool products, pose an increased inhalation risk. Its staying-legal page lists unregistered diatomaceous earth among the things that are not legal.

A registered label is a starting point, not a promise. EPA notes that some bed bug populations have become resistant to pyrethrins and pyrethroids, and the Rutgers authors point to the prevalence of insecticide resistance as one reason alternative products have been developed. For a candid look, see [whether bed bug sprays actually work](/blog/do-bed-bug-sprays-actually-work), and for how heat stacks up against chemicals, see [heat versus chemical bed bug treatment](/blog/heat-vs-chemical-bed-bug-treatment-canada).
What about bleach and other household cleaners?

None of them is a bed bug treatment. [University of Florida Extension's list of things not to do for bed bugs](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/in925) names bleach or other household cleaners among the things not to apply, along with flammable liquids, exterior-only or lawn products applied indoors, moth balls, oils and soaps used on furniture, and store-bought gardening products that claim to kill bugs other than bed bugs.

items: **Bleach.** Florida Extension lists it among the things not to apply, and none of the sources reviewed recommends it.
**Other disinfectant sprays and wipes.** Check each one the way you would check Lysol. If bed bugs are not named in the directions, the label gives no bed bug directions.

**Rubbing alcohol.** EPA lists using rubbing alcohol that is not a registered pesticide product among the things that are not legal, and says it is flammable and has caused numerous house fires when used to control bed bugs. Florida Extension lists alcohol among the flammable liquids not to apply. What university tests found is in [the alcohol guide](/blog/does-alcohol-kill-bed-bugs).

**Oils and soaps.** Florida Extension says oils and soaps used on furniture will not keep bed bugs from climbing up, and the Rutgers results above show how two detergent-based sprays performed even when sold for bed bugs.
**Foggers.** Florida Extension says not to use them because they are ineffective and not a replacement for a proper fumigation.

body.text: Has misusing chemicals for bed bugs made people sick?

Yes. In [a 2011 CDC report](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6037a1.htm), CDC counted 111 illnesses linked to insecticides used against bed bugs in seven states (California, Florida, Michigan, North Carolina, New York, Texas and Washington) between 2003 and 2010. One illness was fatal, 90 of the 111 (81 percent) were low severity, and pyrethroids, pyrethrins or both were involved in 99 (89 percent). Excessive application and failing to wash or change treated bedding were among the most common contributing factors.

Those cases involved insecticides, not disinfectants, but they show what piling chemicals into a bedroom can cost. Florida Extension describes off-label pesticide use as the biggest safety concern that licensed pest professionals see when they are called in after failed home remedies. Anyone who feels unwell after exposure to any of these products should contact a healthcare provider or a poison control center.
What should you do instead of spraying Lysol?
Confirm that the bug is a bed bug, find where the bugs live, and use a method that has directions for bed bugs.

items: **Identify the insect.** [What bed bugs look like at each life stage](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) covers adults, nymphs and eggs. If what you found is small and dark, [the guide to black bed bugs](/blog/black-bed-bugs) explains the black spots and the usual look-alikes, and [bugs that look like bed bugs](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-bed-bugs) compares them side by side. [This guide to bed bug bites](/blog/bed-bug-bites) shows what bites look like and how to tell for sure.
**Find the hiding places.** Work through [where bed bugs hide](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide), starting with the bed.
**Deal with the bed.** [Bed bugs on a mattress](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress) lays out what to do with the mattress itself.
**Choose a treatment.** [How to get rid of bed bugs](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs) follows EPA's integrated approach from confirmation through monitoring.

**Bring in help.** EPA suggests consulting a pest management professional to inspect the residence, and it lists hiring applicators who have little or no bed bug experience or who do not provide a follow-up inspection among the practices that are legal but not safe.

faqs.question: Can I spray Lysol on a mattress to kill bed bugs?
faqs.answer: Not as a bed bug treatment. The label EPA accepted for Lysol Disinfectant Spray in January 2025 lists bedding and a mattress entry among the fabrics it can spot-treat against germs, with directions to spray until wet without saturating. It names no insect, carries a flammability warning and says not to spray in eyes or on skin. No source reviewed tested Lysol on bed bugs in bedding. The mattress guide on this site covers what is usually done instead, including which pesticides are labeled for mattresses.

faqs.question: Does Lysol kill bed bug eggs?
faqs.answer: There is no evidence that it does. The Lysol label makes no claim about insects or eggs. In the nearest controlled test, a 2014 Rutgers University study of products sold for bed bugs, only one of five essential oil sprays killed a high share of eggs, about 87 percent, and the other four had little effect. A disinfectant that was never tested on eggs should not be relied on to remove them.

faqs.question: Does bleach kill bed bugs?
faqs.answer: No source reviewed recommends it. University of Florida Extension lists bleach or other household cleaners among the things not to apply for bed bugs, and it calls off-label pesticide use the biggest safety concern professionals see after failed home remedies. None of the sources reviewed measured what bleach does to a bed bug, and a liquid on a surface faces the same problem as any spray, which is the bugs and eggs hidden out of reach.

faqs.question: Is it illegal to use Lysol on bed bugs?
faqs.answer: The Lysol label states that it is a violation of federal law to use the product in a manner inconsistent with its labeling, and University of Florida Extension says label directions are considered law at the federal and state levels. Spraying Lysol on insects is a use the label does not describe. The more practical point for a homeowner is that the label gives no bed bug directions to follow, and the sources reviewed show no evidence it can end an infestation.

faqs.question: What should I do if I already sprayed Lysol on my bed?
faqs.answer: Stop adding products, and keep sparks, flames and heat sources away from the area, as the label directs for this flammable aerosol. If the spray got in someone's eyes, the label says to rinse slowly with water for 15 to 20 minutes and call a poison control center or doctor. If anyone has symptoms after exposure, contact a healthcare provider. Then confirm that the bugs are bed bugs and move to a method built for them, with a pest professional's help if needed.
